summary: Defines the underlying data model used by SIMPLE presence agents for SIP-based instant messaging and presence. It guides mapping different communication systems into presence documents consistently. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Presence tells others whether you are willing to talk and how to reach you. Earlier rules said how to write that down in a file but left unclear what the parts of the file stand for. This RFC names the three things a presence document describes: the person, the services on offer and the devices those services run on.

subtitle: What the parts of a presence document mean: the person, the services on offer and the devices those services run on.

tldr.problem: Presence documents said how to format status information but not what each part of a document describes, so real communications systems had no consistent way to map themselves into one.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a data model with three components, the person, the service and the device, gives each a set of properties, and maps them onto the PIDF XML format with new person and device elements.
tldr.outcome: A presence document now states which services are on offer, how to reach each one and which device it runs on, and a reader can combine documents from several sources.

today: RFC 4479 is a Proposed Standard. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and the document itself records no later revision of the model it defines.

sections.title: Why a Presence Data Model
sections.content:
Presence is the ability and willingness of a user to communicate across a set of devices. RFC 2778 defines a model and the terminology for presence systems, and RFC 3863 defines the XML document format used to carry presence information. Both model presence information as a series of tuples, where each tuple holds a status, a communications address and other markup. Neither says what a tuple is meant to describe, nor how a real communications system maps into a presence document.

RFC 4479 answers both questions. It defines a presence data model with three data components, the person, the service and the device, and it shows how to map a communications system into a presence document using that model. The model is defined as an extension to the PIDF document format of RFC 3863, so documents that follow it stay compatible with implementations built before the model was complete.

The three components answer three different questions. The person component carries the willingness and the desire to communicate, such as being in a meeting or out to lunch. The service component carries the ability to communicate, because the services are what a user is reachable through. The device component carries the physical platform, which lets a reader correlate services that run on the same hardware. Geographic location illustrates the split: a location is a fact about a person and about a device, but services have no location of their own, so location belongs in the person or device component and never in the service component.
sections.plainLanguage: Presence tells others whether you are willing to talk and how to reach you. Earlier rules described the file format but left unclear what the parts of it were for. This RFC names three parts: the person, the services on offer and the devices those services run on. Each part answers a different question: are you willing, how do I reach you, and where does it run.

sections.title: The Vocabulary of the Model
sections.content:
Beyond the terms of RFC 2778 and RFC 3863, the document defines the words it uses for the parts of a presence document.

  • Device: a physical component a user interacts with to make or receive communications, such as a phone, a PDA or a PC.
  • Service: a form of communication used to interact with the user, such as instant messaging or telephony.
  • Person: the end user, described by states such as busy or sad that affect the ability and willingness to communicate.
  • Occurrence: a single description of one service, one device or one person. There may be several occurrences of the same thing in one document.
  • Presentity: the combination of devices, services and person information that gives a complete picture of a user's presence on the network.
  • Presentity URI: a URI that uniquely identifies a presentity and provides a handle for obtaining presence information about it.
  • Data component: one of the device, service or person parts of a presence document.
  • Status: information about a service, person or device that typically changes over time. Characteristics: information about the same things that is usually fixed over time and descriptive in nature, such as the size of a display.
  • Attribute: a status or a characteristic, in other words a single piece of presence information. A presence attribute means the same thing.
  • Composition: the act of combining presence and event data about a presentity into a coherent picture of its state.
sections.plainLanguage: The document names the parts of a presence document and says which of them change over time. The word to learn is presentity, the thing whose presence is being described, and data component, one of the three parts of the document: person, service or device.

sections.title: Person, Service and Device
sections.content:
Figure 1 draws the model. A presentity, identified by a presentity URI, holds three kinds of data component: the person, the service and the device. Each component carries attributes, and every attribute belongs to the component it describes rather than to the component that reported it. If a cell phone reports that the user is in a meeting, the status in-a-meeting belongs to the person, because it is a fact about the human and not about the handset. The document may also carry information about the cell phone as a device.

The person component models the user, and there is only one per presentity, so it is a facade for a single human being. A customer support help desk can be modelled this way, treated as one person who is busy when no member of staff is available. Person characteristics are the static facts, such as an alias, which is a URI that identifies the same user under a different presentity URI. Person status is the dynamic part: what the user is doing, where the user is, how the user feels. The document notes that the line between static and dynamic information is fuzzy, and the model does not draw it in a way a program could rely on.

Ambiguity is modelled rather than hidden. When several sources describe the same service, device or person, each component can carry several occurrences, and each occurrence has its own occurrence identifier, unique across the services, devices and person elements of that document. The identifier is meant to persist over time, because it is used to set composition and authorization policies. Notes and timestamps help a reader resolve the ambiguity: the timestamp gives the time of the most recent change, and the component that changed most recently can be treated as the more reliable source. The document does not require any particular resolution algorithm.

The presentity URI identifies the whole thing. A presentity may have more than one, for example a URI from the pres scheme, a SIP URI or an XMPP IRI, or several aliases in one domain that are all equivalent identifiers. When a document is built, the presentity URI is ideally the identifier that was used to request the document, since the requester may not know about the other identifiers. The URI is independent of the services and devices the presentity has, and it is not only a name: it represents a resource that can be subscribed to, which is what makes the presentity URI a form of one-number communications.
sections.plainLanguage: Each part of a presence document is about one thing: the person, one service or one device. Information goes with the thing it describes, not with the thing that happened to report it. When two sources disagree about the same service or device, the document can hold several versions of it, each with its own identifier, and leaves the choice to the reader.

sections.title: What a Service Carries
sections.content:
The document does not fix a list of service types, because a service is hard to define precisely. One definition fails when a service is spread across several programs or devices, and another fails when several programs share one address. Instead, anything may be treated as a service as long as it carries the properties the model requires: characteristics that identify its nature and capabilities, reach information that says how to contact it, status that gives its current state, and relative information that relates it to the other services of the presentity. Because of this, there is no central registry of services and no single attribute with values such as telephony.

Characteristics describe what a watcher gets when the service is used. Their purpose is to help the watcher choose, because listing several services in one document is an explicit offer of a choice. Capabilities, such as the media that might be used or the direction of communication allowed, are part of the characteristics. One important characteristic is the list of devices on which the service runs, identified by device ID, which lets a reader tell which services run on the same hardware even when the document carries no device information of its own. A document may also list a single service only, which means the presentity is not offering a choice.

Relative information is the priority the user gives each service. The priorities are relative to each other and have no meaning as absolute numbers, so two services with priorities of 1 and .5 are the same as two services with priorities of .2 and .1. The priority says: if you cannot decide which to use, use these in this order.

Status is the dynamic part of a service. The simplest form is a basic status with two values, closed and open. Closed means a communication attempt will probably fail, will not reach the intended party, or will not produce the communications the characteristics describe. A call forwarded to voicemail when the user is busy is closed, and so is a hotel room telephone number that still rings after checkout, because the call reaches the next guest. Open means the opposite, that the attempt will probably succeed and reach the desired target. Status can also depend on the session that is set up, so a softphone service can be available for instant messaging and unavailable for audio. Only dynamic state that helps a watcher decide whether and when to contact the service belongs in the document: whether a cell phone has strong or merely good signal does not pass that test.
sections.plainLanguage: A service is anything the user can be reached through, such as a phone line or an instant messaging account. The document does not list service types. Each service instead has to say what it is, how to reach it, how it is doing, and how the user prefers it compared with the other services. Its status is simply open or closed.

sections.title: Reach Information and the Service URI
sections.content:
Reach information tells the reader how to contact a service. For a service reachable over a network it includes a service URI that can be used to reach the service. A URI alone is often enough, but not always. Two applications in one mobile phone may share one SIP address of record, and the application that answers depends on the type of body in the request. A service may also hold application logic that works only when contacted from matching software. When more than the URI is needed, the service carries extra attributes, and these must be understood for the service to be used at all. A watcher that receives reach information it does not understand should discard the service information.

Reach information identifies the service, so each service in a document needs a distinct set of it, otherwise the reader would have no way to choose between them. This is also the test for whether something counts as one service or several: something cannot be a service unless there is a way to reach it separately from another service. A softphone that handles both audio and video is one service, because a video-only version could not be reached on its own. A service may still be listed with no reach information at all, which says the service exists but is not on offer, for example a telephone number given only so watchers know the user is busy.

The reach information is a weak contract, not a guarantee. The document may model a group of real services, so a connection with all the described characteristics may not be possible, and the preferences of the presentity always come first, so a caller asking for the video service may be connected to another one. The same service may be reachable through many URIs, and different watchers may be given different URIs, or the URI for one watcher may change over time. The document notes that this lets the recipient of a communications attempt work out the context in which the attempt was made, which can be used as a technique against unwanted communications.
sections.plainLanguage: Reach information is how to contact one service, usually a single address such as a SIP URI. When the address alone is not enough, the service carries extra instructions that the reader has to understand, and a reader that does not understand them should drop that service. The address is a promise, not a guarantee, because the user can still prefer to connect the caller somewhere else.

sections.title: Devices and Device Identifiers
sections.content:
A device models the physical environment in which services run: a cell phone, a PC, a laptop, a consumer telephone, a PBX extension or a dispatch console. The mapping between services and devices is many to many. One service can run on several devices, as when two SIP phones register against a single address of record, and one device can carry several services, as a cell phone carrying telephony, SMS and MMS. A device may carry no service at all, which is how an RFID tag can be described: it has properties such as location, and a compositor that finds a video telephone tagged with the same RFID can use the tag's location to say something about where the video telephone is. The device is a model of the system, so a PC running services inside a virtual machine can be described as two devices.

Each device has a device ID, a URI that is a globally and temporally unique identifier, and in this model a URN. The identifier should also be readily computable, so that different systems are likely to refer to the same device with the same ID, because that is what allows information about a device from several sources to be combined. No single URN scheme suits every device, so more than one is expected. The Electronic Serial Number works for cellular telephones and the MAC address for IP devices, but the MAC address changes if the interface card changes, and neither is yet tied to a URN scheme.

In the meantime a UUID URN is used. For devices with a MAC address, version 1 UUIDs are recommended, since they are time based and make use of the MAC address; for devices without one, version 4 UUIDs are recommended, since they are purely random and give uniqueness. The UUID would normally be chosen at manufacture and stored in flash or other non-volatile memory. A UUID has the properties of being globally and temporally unique, but because of its random component it cannot be readily computed, so it cannot serve as a correlation identifier with other presence sources on the network. The document expects later specifications to provide better device identifiers.

Device characteristics describe the physical device, such as its display size, processor speed and memory. Device status is the dynamic part, such as whether the device is powered on, how much battery power remains and where the device is. These are reported so the user can choose a service, and they cannot be used to infer the nature of the service: a fast processor does not mean the video quality on that device will be good, because other constraints may reduce the processor available to that service. Likewise, the state of a device does not by itself set the state of a service, unless the consumer of the document knows otherwise.
sections.plainLanguage: A device is the box the services run on: a phone, a PC, a console. Each device gets a device ID, which is a URN, and the ID should be easy for different programs to calculate the same way, so information from several sources can be joined. The document suggests a UUID URN for now and notes that it cannot be calculated, so joining needs another method.

sections.title: Mapping the Model onto PIDF
sections.content:
Presence data is carried in the PIDF format of RFC 3863. The presence element holds the information for the presentity, and its entity attribute holds the presentity URI. The existing tuple element represents a service, which keeps the mapping compatible with implementations built before this model existed, and the contact element inside the tuple holds the service URI. New presence attributes appear directly as children of tuple. Attributes defined before this document, such as basic, stay as children of status, so a service attribute can appear under either element but never under both. The id attribute of the tuple carries the service occurrence.

The document introduces a person element and a device element, both of which may appear zero or more times as children of presence, each with a mandatory id attribute holding its occurrence identifier. The person element carries status and characteristic elements, then optional note elements and an optional timestamp. The device element carries its own elements, then a deviceID element holding the URN for the device, then notes and a timestamp. Notes that are direct children of presence apply to every person occurrence that has no note of its own. A client that does not understand the new elements ignores them, and because the meaning of a service matches the meaning of a tuple in RFC 2778 and RFC 3863, documents using this model stay compliant with older implementations. The two schemas are split into a common schema, common-schema.xsd, and the data model, data-model.xsd.

Two rules about attributes matter. A missing attribute says nothing at all, following the same idea as the capability declarations of RFC 3840: the watcher cannot conclude anything about its value, whether it was withheld or is unsupported, so a presence document is at its best when it carries as many attributes as the presentity is willing and able to provide. And the line between status and characteristics is conceptual only. Nothing in a document marks an attribute as one or the other, and any presence attribute may change at any time, but all future presence attributes must be defined as children of tuple rather than of status, and the schemas here define no status element for the person and device elements.

Extensions add presence attributes, and the document sets out three questions an extension has to answer: which data components the new attribute applies to and what it means in each, whether it belongs in a new namespace or an existing one, and whether the extension itself needs points of extension, which must then be marked in the schema with the any construct. The worked example in Section 7 models an instant messaging client, where the note and the pre-defined status messages belong to the person, the service tuple publishes the client's address of record and carries no characteristics, and the idle indicator belongs to the device because idleness describes use of the device rather than of the service.
sections.plainLanguage: The model is written into the XML format defined earlier for presence documents. A service becomes a tuple element, a person and a device each get their own element with an identifier, and the device carries its identifier in a deviceID element. A missing attribute means nothing at all, so a document should carry as much as it can.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The presence information described by this model is very sensitive, and privacy filtering plays a key role in processing it. Privacy filtering is the act of applying permissions to a presence document in order to remove information a watcher is not authorized to see, and in more general terms it is a form of authorization. It can also ensure that a watcher sees no presence data at all for a presentity, and it can even ensure that the presentity does not know it is being blocked. The SIP presence specifications of RFC 3856 require this authorization processing to be performed before presence information is divulged, and separate specifications define how authorization policies are conveyed to presence servers.

Integrity of presence information is equally critical. An attacker who modifies presence data can divert communications, for example by changing the address a service is reachable at. The protocols used to transport presence data, such as SIP for presence, are relied on to provide the necessary integrity functions.

The document also has internationalization considerations. The data model mostly contains tokens meant for programs rather than for people, and programs are expected to translate those tokens into text in the language the watcher prefers. The note element can hold free text, so it and other free-text elements should carry the xml:lang attribute, and the document allows several note elements so the same note can be given in several languages and scripts. Without that attribute the default value is i-default. Because the model is XML, it carries the Unicode character set natively, and use of UTF-8 is recommended where parser encoding support is inconsistent.
sections.plainLanguage: Presence information says where someone is and how to reach them, so it is treated as sensitive. Before a document is sent, a server filters it, removing the parts the watcher is not allowed to see, and it can even hide the fact that the watcher is blocked. The document also has to arrive unaltered, because a changed address would send calls to the wrong place.

data.title: Presence document for an instant messaging client
data.code:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<presence xmlns="urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:pidf"
 xmlns:dm="urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:pidf:data-model"
 xmlns:rp="urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:pidf:rpid"
 xmlns:caps="urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:pidf:caps">
 <tuple id="sg89ae">
  <status>
   <basic>open</basic>
  </status>
  <dm:deviceID>mac:8asd7d7d70</dm:deviceID>
  <contact>sip:someone@example.com</contact>
 </tuple>
 <dm:person id="p1">
  <rp:activities>
   <rp:on-the-phone/>
  </rp:activities>
 </dm:person>
 <dm:device id="pc122">
  <rp:user-input>idle</rp:user-input>
  <dm:deviceID>mac:8asd7d7d70</dm:deviceID>
 </dm:device>
</presence>
